page.probe.title: Check a host
diag.probe.title: Check a host
diag.probe.text: Ping, route, DNS, TCP and TLS to a site or address
probe.note: The service runs the checks and changes nothing in the network. The host is not written to the log.
probe.error.target: Enter an IP or a host name, for example example.com.
probe.error.port: Port is a number from 1 to 65535.
probe.error.service: The service did not answer — it runs the checks. Start the service and try again.
probe.method.ping: Four ICMP echoes, one per second. Many hosts and routers do not answer echoes — the site may still open.
probe.method.trace: Route — ICMP echoes with a growing packet lifetime: routers along the way answer. An asterisk means a router stayed silent, not a break.
probe.method.dns: Lookup through the system DNS — programs get the same addresses.
probe.method.tcp: A TCP connection without data: the port is open if the host answered the handshake.
probe.method.tls: A TLS handshake without sending data: version, cipher and certificate. Certificate revocation is not checked.
probe.path.proxy: Proxy mode: the service measures directly, bypassing the server.
probe.path.vpn: Protection is on: the check goes through the tunnel and the server.
probe.path.vpnIcmp: Protection is on: echoes go into the tunnel, and proxy protocols do not carry ICMP — there may be no answer even though the site opens.

page.compare.title: Before and after VPN
diag.compare.title: Before and after VPN
diag.compare.text: Addresses, WebRTC, route and DNS before protection and now
compare.unavailable: The service did not answer — it does the comparing. Start the service and try again.
compare.before.taken: Before — taken when protection was turned on {0}
compare.before.none: There is no “before” snapshot: the service takes it when protection is turned on. Turn protection on — and compare.
compare.method.ip: The address the Cloudflare check site (1.1.1.1/cdn-cgi/trace) reports for the service's request — by the same way programs go. Sites opened around protection (split mode) see another address.
compare.method.ipv6: The same check site by its IPv6 address. No answer means IPv6 is closed or the network has none: that is not a leak.
compare.method.webrtc: A STUN request to a Cloudflare server over UDP — the way a browser learns its address for calls and video. A browser may behave differently: it hides local addresses behind mDNS, and in proxy mode sends WebRTC UDP around the proxy — then sites see the real address.
compare.method.route: The adapter the system picks for an internet address, honoring the tunnel rules, and its gateway.
compare.method.dns: DNS servers assigned to the outgoing adapter. Whether DNS queries go around the tunnel is measured by the Check page — the DNS row.
page.path.title: Path to a site
diag.path.title: Path to a site
diag.path.text: Computer → router → provider → VPN → site: what is measured and what is assumed
path.node.adapter.unknown: The service did not name the outgoing adapter
path.link.inside: Inside the computer: app → OS network stack
path.link.inside.vpn: Inside the computer: app → TUN adapter → the core encrypts
path.link.wifi: Over Wi-Fi radio to the router
path.link.lan: Over cable or local network to the router
path.note.off: Protection is off: traffic goes from the provider straight to the site. “Check the site” measures this path with a TLS handshake and a traceroute.
path.note.proxy: Proxy mode: apps that use the proxy go through the server, the rest go directly. The site check bypasses the server, so the server-to-site segment stays assumed.
path.note.vpn: VPN mode: all traffic of the machine goes into the tunnel — the router and the provider only see an encrypted stream to the server. A traceroute through the tunnel does not measure the router or the provider.
path.measured.title: Measured
path.measured.text: Solid line: the point or segment is backed by OS data or a measurement — the gateway address, a hop reply, the exit address, a handshake with the site.
path.conditional.title: Assumed
path.conditional.text: Dashed line: this is almost always how it works, but the segment was not measured. “Check the site” and “Who are the providers” turn assumptions into measurements where possible.
path.tunnel.title: Inside the tunnel
path.tunnel.text: Line in the protection color: the segment runs inside the tunnel — the router and the provider only see an encrypted stream to the server, not the sites.
page.layers.title: How the network works
diag.layers.title: How the network works
diag.layers.text: The seven OSI layers and protocols — on this machine's data
layers.note: Values come from this machine right now, supplied by the service. “Not measured” means the service did not provide them: explanations never put a typical value in place of a measurement.
layers.protocols.label: Protocols
layer.7.name: Application
layer.7.text: Apps say what they want: open a page (HTTP), find an address by name (DNS).
layer.7.expert: VPN protocols live here too — VLESS, Trojan, Shadowsocks: to the network they are ordinary apps carrying other packets inside their data.
layer.6.name: Presentation
layer.6.text: How data is encoded and protected: TLS encrypts the page so it cannot be read or altered on the way.
layer.6.expert: TCP/IP has no separate layers 5–7: TLS and HTTP live inside the app. OSI is useful as a map of where things happen.
layer.5.name: Session
layer.5.text: Keeps the conversation going: start, continue, finish. On the internet TCP and TLS do this — there is usually no separate protocol.
layer.5.expert: A TLS session can resume without a full handshake (session tickets), and HTTP/2 carries many requests over one connection.
layer.4.name: Transport
layer.4.text: Delivery between apps by port numbers: TCP is reliable and ordered, UDP is fast with no guarantees.
layer.4.expert: A port is 16 bits: 443 is HTTPS, 53 is DNS. Address and port on both ends plus the protocol identify a connection.
layer.3.name: Network
layer.3.text: IP addresses and routes: how a packet finds its way across many networks to the right computer.
layer.3.expert: Every router on the way looks only at the destination and its routing table; TTL drops by 1 at each one — traceroute is built on that.
layer.2.name: Data link
layer.2.text: Delivery within one network by MAC address: from the computer to the router.
layer.2.expert: MTU is the largest frame that passes without splitting, usually 1500 bytes. The computer learns the router's MAC via ARP (IPv4) or NDP (IPv6).
layer.1.name: Physical
layer.1.text: The signal itself: Wi-Fi radio, current in a cable, light in fiber, cellular.
layer.1.expert: Adapter speed is the link speed to the router, not to the site: further on the slowest segment of the path sets the limit.
layer.1.protocols: Wi-Fi radio, copper, fiber, LTE and 5G
fact.tunnel.none: none — protection is off or in proxy mode
layers.tunnel.title: VPN across the layers: a packet in a packet
layers.tunnel.text: In VPN mode an app hands a packet (layer 3) to the TUN adapter. The core wraps it in the VPN protocol (layer 7), encrypts it with TLS (layer 6) and carries it over TCP or UDP (layer 4) to the server. The router and the provider only see the outer packet — to the server.
layers.tunnel.expert: The outer packet is bigger than the inner one by the IP, TCP or UDP, TLS and VPN protocol headers — that is why the tunnel MTU is smaller than the adapter's. The server unwraps the packet and sends it to the site from its own address.
layers.tunnel.on: the tunnel is on — all traffic of the machine goes this way
layers.tunnel.proxy: proxy mode — only apps using the proxy go this way, without the TUN adapter
layers.tunnel.off: protection is off — packets go as they are
topic.ip.title: IP address
topic.ip.text: The computer's number in a network. At home it is private — the router gave it; on the internet sites see a shared address: the provider's router or the VPN server.
topic.ip.expert: IPv4 is 32 bits, IPv6 is 128. Private ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) never reach the internet: the router replaces them with its own address (NAT). The /24 prefix is how many address bits define the network.
topic.transport.title: TCP and UDP
topic.transport.text: TCP is like registered mail: a connection, receipts, resending what was lost. UDP is like a postcard: fast with no receipts; calls, games, DNS and QUIC use it.
topic.transport.expert: TCP opens with a three-way handshake SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK and keeps order and a send window; UDP has only an 8-byte header with ports and length.
topic.dns.title: DNS
topic.dns.text: The internet's phone book: turns the name example.com into an IP address. Whoever sees your DNS queries knows which sites you open.
topic.dns.expert: A query is usually UDP to port 53; the answer is cached for its TTL. In VPN mode the OS asks DNS through the tunnel (172.19.0.2): the core answers with a FakeDNS placeholder (198.18.0.0/15) and resolves the real address on the server — the query never reaches the provider.
topic.tls.title: TLS
topic.tls.text: The padlock in the address bar: encrypts the data and checks by certificate that you are talking to the real site.
topic.tls.expert: A TLS 1.3 handshake takes one round trip: a shared key via ECDHE, the certificate checked along the chain to a root authority. The site name (SNI) at the start of the handshake is visible to the provider unless the site hides it with ECH.
topic.http.title: HTTP and HTTPS
topic.http.text: HTTP is the language of page requests: “give me the page” — “here it is”. HTTPS is the same HTTP inside TLS: the provider sees which site you talk to, but not what is on the page.
topic.http.expert: HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 run over TCP with TLS on port 443, HTTP/3 over QUIC on UDP. Under VPN the provider does not even see the site name — only an encrypted stream to the server.
topic.tun.title: TUN
topic.tun.text: A virtual network card. In VPN mode the OS hands it all traffic, and the protection app encrypts it and sends it to the server through the real adapter.
topic.tun.expert: TUN works at layer 3 — it takes IP packets. Routes 0.0.0.0/1 and 128.0.0.0/1 are more specific than the default route, so the OS picks the tunnel without removing the old route.
topic.routing.title: Routing
topic.routing.text: Choosing the road: for every packet the OS looks up the routing table to find the adapter and gateway to send it through.
topic.routing.expert: The most specific route wins (longest prefix), with equal ones the lower metric. The default route means “everything else”, usually to the router.
page.events.title: Network events
diag.events.title: Network events
diag.events.text: What happened to protection and the network — and why
events.note: Events since the window started: the service reports the state, the lab explains what happened in the network.
events.empty: No events yet. Turn protection on or off — what happened in the network and why will appear here.
event.connecting.title: Connecting
event.connecting.text: The service checks the server and starts the core. Until the tunnel is up, the kill switch, if on, keeps the network closed — nothing slips past.
event.connecting.expert: The service resolves the server, builds and validates the core config (Xray, plus sing-box for TUN), starts it, then sets routes and firewall rules.
event.connected.title: Protection is on
event.connected.text: The tunnel is up: all traffic of the machine goes through the server, sites see its address and the provider sees only an encrypted stream.
event.connected.expert: The TUN adapter got routes 0.0.0.0/1 and 128.0.0.0/1, the OS DNS is 172.19.0.2 inside the tunnel; the service made sure the server answers through the tunnel.
event.proxyOn.title: Proxy is on
event.proxyOn.text: Apps that use the proxy go through the server (the browser — via the system proxy). The rest go directly.
event.proxyOn.expert: The core listens for SOCKS and HTTP on 127.0.0.1 and the OS got the system proxy address. There is no TUN and no firewall rules: an app without the proxy bypasses the server.
event.reconnecting.title: Reconnecting — attempt {0}
event.reconnecting.text: The connection to the server was lost. The service tries again; the kill switch, if on, holds traffic until the tunnel is back.
event.reconnecting.expert: The check through the tunnel got no answer; the service restarts the connection with a growing pause between attempts and keeps the firewall rules.
event.blocked.title: Network closed
event.blocked.text: The server does not answer and the kill switch holds traffic: no internet, but no leak either.
event.blocked.expert: Firewall rules let through only traffic to the server and the allowed local network. The error code is in the row, details are in the Check journal.
event.error.title: Error
event.error.text: The service or the core stopped with an error. If the kill switch is on, the network stays closed until the error is fixed.
event.error.expert: The error code is in the row, details are in the Check journal.
event.off.title: Protection is off
event.off.text: No tunnel: traffic goes directly through the provider, sites see your real address.
event.off.expert: The service stopped the core and removed the tunnel routes and firewall rules; the OS DNS is the adapter's again.
event.strictBlock.title: Strict mode block
event.strictBlock.text: Protection was turned off, but strict mode keeps the network closed until you connect or turn it off.
event.strictBlock.expert: Firewall rules stay, there is no tunnel — nothing goes out except what is allowed.
event.paused.title: Pause for Wi-Fi sign-in
event.paused.text: Protection briefly lets traffic bypass the tunnel so the network's sign-in page can open — in a hotel, café or train.
event.paused.expert: The service opens the firewall for the pause; then the tunnel and the block come back on their own.
event.resumed.title: Pause ended
event.resumed.text: Protection holds traffic again: nothing bypasses the tunnel.
event.resumed.expert: Firewall rules are back; traffic goes only through the tunnel again.
event.networkChanged.title: Network changed
event.networkChanged.text: Another Wi-Fi, cable or address. The service checks the tunnel again: old connections may have dropped — apps will reopen them.
event.networkChanged.expert: The OS changed the default route or the adapter address; the service routes the server address through the new gateway again.
event.exitMeasured.title: Address seen by sites: {0}
event.exitMeasured.text: The service asked a check site the same way apps go: sites see this address.
event.exitMeasured.expert: The request to 1.1.1.1/cdn-cgi/trace goes through the core — the same way as app traffic; this is a measurement, not the address from the server settings.
event.warning.title: The check found a problem
event.warning.text: {0}. Open Check for details and what to do.
event.warning.expert: This is a measurement by the service after connecting, not a model: the check saw traffic going the wrong way.
event.warning.allTraffic: Not all traffic goes through the tunnel
event.warning.killSwitch: The kill switch does not hold
page.trouble.title: Why a site does not open
diag.trouble.title: Why a site does not open
diag.trouble.text: Step by step: network, protection, DNS, connection, TLS
trouble.note: The check goes the way a browser request does: network → protection → DNS → connection → TLS. The first failed step is the cause and later ones are not checked: a measurement makes the call, not a guess.
trouble.via.off: Protection is off: measurements go directly — the way apps go.
trouble.via.vpn: VPN mode: measurements go through the tunnel and the server — the way apps go.
trouble.via.proxy: Proxy mode: measurements go directly, bypassing the server, while a browser with the proxy goes through the server — results may differ.
trouble.noAdapter: no adapter that is up with a route to the internet
trouble.step.network.title: Machine network
trouble.step.network.text: There is an adapter that is up with internet access — usually through the router.
trouble.step.network.expert: The service reads the OS adapters and routing table: it needs an adapter that is up (not a tunnel) with a default route or a gateway; a cellular modem may have no gateway.
trouble.step.protection.title: Protection
trouble.step.protection.text: Protection is not keeping the network closed: kill switch, strict mode or connecting.
trouble.step.protection.expert: While protection connects, reconnects or blocks, firewall rules let through only traffic to the server.
trouble.step.dns.title: DNS
trouble.step.dns.text: The site name turns into an address.
trouble.step.dns.expert: The service asks the system DNS — the same way apps do; in VPN mode that is the DNS inside the tunnel.
trouble.step.tcp.title: Connection
trouble.step.tcp.text: The site accepts a TCP connection on port 443.
trouble.step.tcp.expert: Three-way handshake SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK: a refusal means the host answered RST, silence means the answer got lost or was cut on the way.
trouble.step.tls.title: TLS
trouble.step.tls.text: The handshake completes and the certificate proves it is the right site.
trouble.step.tls.expert: The service checks the certificate chain to a trusted authority, the name and the dates — like a browser; revocation is not checked.
trouble.verdict.noService.title: The service did not answer
trouble.verdict.noService.text: The service does the measuring — without it there is nothing to go on.
trouble.verdict.noService.todo: Start the service and run the check again.
trouble.verdict.noNetwork.title: No internet access
trouble.verdict.noNetwork.text: The machine has no adapter that is up with a route to the internet — the site is not the problem.
trouble.verdict.noNetwork.todo: Check Wi-Fi or the cable and reconnect to the network.
trouble.verdict.protectionBlocks.title: Protection keeps the network closed
trouble.verdict.protectionBlocks.text: Protection keeps the network closed: that is how the kill switch stops traffic from bypassing the tunnel.
trouble.verdict.protectionBlocks.todo: Wait for the connection or pick another server. To go online without protection, turn it off (and strict mode).
trouble.verdict.nameNotFound.title: No such name
trouble.verdict.nameNotFound.text: DNS answered that the name does not exist: a typo in the address or the site is gone.
trouble.verdict.nameNotFound.todo: Check the address. If it is right, the site has probably shut down.
trouble.verdict.dnsFailed.title: DNS did not answer
trouble.verdict.dnsFailed.text: The name query got no answer: the DNS server is unreachable or queries are blocked.
trouble.verdict.dnsFailed.todo: Under protection, switch servers. Without protection, check DNS in Protection and leaks or turn protection on.
trouble.verdict.portRefused.title: The site refused the connection
trouble.verdict.portRefused.text: The host refused port 443: the site does not accept HTTPS or is down.
trouble.verdict.portRefused.todo: Try later: the site may be under maintenance.
trouble.verdict.noAnswer.title: The site did not answer
trouble.verdict.noAnswer.text: The connection went out and no answer came: the site is overloaded or the connection is cut on the way.
trouble.verdict.noAnswer.todo: Under protection, switch servers. Without protection, turn it on: if the site opens then, the provider is cutting the path.
trouble.verdict.unreachable.title: No route to the site
trouble.verdict.unreachable.text: The network reported there is no way to this host.
trouble.verdict.unreachable.todo: Check the network; under protection, switch servers.
trouble.verdict.certificate.title: The certificate is not right
trouble.verdict.certificate.text: The site answered, but its certificate does not prove it: expired, issued to another name or by an unknown authority.
trouble.verdict.certificate.todo: Do not enter passwords there. On a public network spoofing is likely — turn protection on and check again.
trouble.verdict.tlsFailed.title: The TLS handshake failed
trouble.verdict.tlsFailed.text: There is a connection, but TLS did not agree: filtering by site name (SNI) or a fault on the site.
trouble.verdict.tlsFailed.todo: Under protection, switch servers. Without protection, turn it on: then the provider does not see the site name.
trouble.verdict.siteAnswers.title: The site answers
trouble.verdict.siteAnswers.text: Network, DNS, connection and TLS are fine — the browser or the site itself is most likely the cause.
trouble.verdict.siteAnswers.todo: Reload the page, clear the cache or try another browser. In proxy mode, check that the browser goes through the proxy.

about.privacy.text:
Private Gateway Client collects no telemetry and sends the developer nothing about you or your connections.

The app talks only to the servers you added, to your subscription addresses (by default only through the VPN) and, when checking for leaks, to address-checking services.

Server keys and subscription addresses live in the OS store, logs stay on this computer without secrets. The support report is anonymized, and you send it yourself.
